content: It is formatted in a citation style commonly used in academic or medical literature. 1. JM et al. investigated the relationship between hormonal contraceptive use, herpes simplex virus infection, and the risk of acquiring HIV-1 among Kenyan women. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2007. 2. Stringer EM and colleagues conducted a multicountry cohort analysis under the MTCT-Plus Initiative to explore the impact of hormonal contraception on HIV disease progression. This study was published in AIDS in 2009. 3. Polis CB et al. examined the effect of hormonal contraceptive use on HIV progression in female seroconverters in Rakai, Uganda. Their research was published in AIDS in 2010. 4. Morrison CS and colleagues studied the progression of HIV disease among women in Uganda and Zimbabwe who used hormonal contraceptives. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2011. 5. Kilmarx PH et al. analyzed disease progression and survival in female sex workers in Thailand infected with HIV-1 subtype E. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2000. 6. Heffron R and colleagues explored the association between hormonal contraceptive use and the risk of HIV-1 disease progression. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2013. 7. Allen S et al. investigated the impact of pregnancy and hormonal contraceptive use on HIV-related mortality in Rwanda. This study was published in the Journal of Women’s Health in 2007. 8. A study group for the MRC Collaborative Study of HIV Infection in Women examined the survival and progression of HIV disease in women attending GUM/HIV clinics in Britain and Ireland. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 1999. 9. Stringer EM et al. conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized trial to assess HIV disease progression by hormonal contraceptive method. This study was published in AIDS. 10. Stringer EM and colleagues compared the intrauterine contraceptive device with hormonal contraception in HIV-infected women in a randomized trial. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2007. 11. Lutalo T et al. studied the effects of hormonal contraceptive use on HIV acquisition and transmission among HIV-discordant couples. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2013. 12. Richardson BA et al. examined the progression of HIV-1 disease among postpartum Kenyan women using hormonal contraception. This study was published in AIDS in 2007. 13. Kreiss J et al. investigated the association between cervical inflammation and the shedding of HIV DNA in cervical secretions. Their findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1994. 14. Graham SM et al. identified antiretroviral adherence and drug resistance as predictors of genital HIV-1 shedding among women initiating treatment. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2010. 15. Clemetson DB et al. studied the detection of HIV DNA in cervical and vaginal secretions and its prevalence among women in Nairobi, Kenya. Their findings were published in JAMA in 1993. 16. Clark RA et al. found no association between genital tract HIV-1 RNA shedding and hormonal contraceptive use in a cohort of Louisiana women. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2007. 17. Cejtin HE et al. examined the effect of hormonal contraceptive use on plasma HIV-1 RNA levels in HIV-infected women. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2003. 18. Kovacs A et al. identified determinants of HIV-1 shedding in the genital tract of women. This study was published in The Lancet in 2001. 19. Kumwenda JJ et al. studied the natural history and risk factors associated with early and established HIV-1 infection among reproductive-age women in Malawi. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2008. 20. Lavreys L et al. investigated the impact of injectable contraceptive use and genital ulcer disease on plasma viral load during early HIV-1 infection in women. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2004. 21. Morrison CS et al. analyzed plasma and cervical viral loads among Ugandan and Zimbabwean women during acute and early HIV-1 infection. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2010. 22. Mostad SB et al. explored the relationship between hormonal contraception, vitamin A deficiency, and the shedding of HIV-1-infected cells from the cervix and vagina. This study was published in The Lancet in 1997. 23. Roccio M et al. studied the effect of low-dose combined oral contraceptives on cervicovaginal shedding of HIV. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2011. 24. Sagar M et al. identified modifiable factors affecting the genetic diversity of the transmitted HIV-1 population. This study was published in AIDS in 2004. 25. Seck K et al. examined the prevalence and risk factors of cervicovaginal HIV shedding among HIV-1 and HIV-2 infected women in Dakar, Senegal. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2001. 26. Tanton C et al. identified correlates of HIV-1 genital shedding in Tanzanian women. This study was published in PLoS One in 2011. 27. Tagy AH et al. compared the effects of low-dose oral contraceptive pills and injectable contraceptives on liver function tests in women with compensated bilharzial liver fibrosis. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2001. 28. Sy FS et al. studied the effect of oral contraceptives on liver function tests in women with schistosomiasis in the Philippines. This study was published in Contraception in 1986. 29. Shaaban MM et al. investigated the effect of oral contraception on serum bile acid levels. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 1984. 30. Shaaban MM et al. examined the effects of oral contraception on liver function tests and serum proteins in women with active schistosomiasis. This study was published in Contraception in 1982. 31. Gad-el-Mawla N et al. studied plasma lipids and lipoproteins in bilharzial females during oral contraceptive therapy. Their findings were published in the Journal of the Egyptian Medical Association in 1972. 32. Gad-el-Mawla N et al. investigated liver function in bilharzial females receiving contraceptive pills. This study was published in Acta Hepato-Splenologica in 1969. 33. El Raghby I et al. examined contraceptive steroid concentrations in women with early active schistosomiasis and the lack of effect of antischistosomal drugs. Their findings were published in Contraception. 34. Beck P et al. compared mechanisms underlying carbohydrate intolerance in subclinical diabetic women during pregnancy and postpartum oral contraceptive steroid treatment. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism in 1969. 35. Kjos SL et al. investigated the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus in Latina women with prior gestational diabetes mellitus using contraception. Their findings were published in JAMA in 1998. 36. Kung AW et al. studied glucose and lipid metabolism with triphasic oral contraceptives in women with a history of gestational diabetes. This study was published in Contraception in 1987. 37. Radberg T et al. conducted metabolic studies in gestational diabetic women during contraceptive treatment, focusing on glucose tolerance and serum lipid composition. Their findings were published in Gynecologic and Obstetric Investigation in 1982. 38. Skouby SO et al. assessed oral contraception and insulin sensitivity in normal women and those with previous gestational diabetes. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism in 1987. 39. Skouby SO et al. studied low-dosage oral contraception in women with previous gestational diabetes. Their findings were published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1982. 40. Xiang AH et al. examined the risk of type 2 diabetes in Latino women with prior gestational diabetes using long-acting injectable progestin contraception. This study was published in Diabetes Care in 2006. 41. Skouby SO et al. investigated oral contraceptives and insulin receptor binding in normal women and those with previous gestational diabetes. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1986. 42. Kjos SL et al. studied the effect of low-dose oral contraceptives on carbohydrate and lipid metabolism in women with recent gestational diabetes. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1990. 43. Radberg T et al. conducted metabolic studies in women with previous gestational diabetes during contraceptive treatment, focusing on serum lipids and high-density lipoproteins. Their findings were published in Acta Endocrinologica in 1982. 44. Skouby SO et al. examined the metabolic effects of triphasic oral contraception in normal women and those with previous gestational diabetes. This study was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1985. 45. Beck P et al. studied the effect of contraceptive steroids on arginine-stimulated glucagon and insulin secretion in women. Their findings were published in Metabolism in 1976. 46. Diab KM et al. compared the metabolic effects of Norplant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, low-dose oral contraceptive pills, and CuT380A in diabetic women. This study was published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology Research in 2000. 47. Garg SK et al. investigated oral contraceptives and renal and retinal complications in young women with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Their findings were published in JAMA in 1994. 48. Grigoryan OR et al. studied contraception in perimenopausal women with diabetes mellitus. Their findings were published in Gynecologic Endocrinology in 2006. 49. Margolis KL et al. conducted a prospective study on oral contraceptive use and the risk of myocardial infarction among Swedish women. This study was published in Fertility and Sterility in 2007. 50. Petersen KR et al. examined the balance of coagulation activity with fibrinolysis during oral contraceptive use in women with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Fertility in 1995. 51. Radberg T et al. conducted a cross-over study on serum and high-density lipoprotein lipids and diabetes control during progestogen and combined estrogen/progestogen contraception in diabetic women. Their findings were published in Hormone and Metabolic Research in 1982. 52. Petersen KR et al. assessed endothelial function during oral contraception in women with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. This study was published in Metabolism in 1994. 53. Di Martino V et al. studied the progression of liver fibrosis in women infected with hepatitis C and the long-term benefit of estrogen exposure. Their findings were published in Hepatology in 2004. 54. Libbrecht L et al. examined the predictive value of liver cell dysplasia for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with chronic viral hepatitis. This study was published in Histopathology in 2001. 55. Eisalo A et al. studied oral contraceptives after liver disease. Their findings were published in the British Medical Journal in 1971. 56. Wang P et al. investigated the safety of hormonal steroid contraceptive use for hepatitis B virus carrier women. Their findings were published in Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety. 57. Schweitzer IL et al. studied oral contraceptives in acute viral hepatitis. Their findings were published in JAMA in 1975. 58. Kapp N et al. conducted a systematic review on the effects of hormonal contraceptive use among women with viral hepatitis or liver cirrhosis. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2009. 59. Mathieu D et al. studied oral contraceptive use and focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver. Their findings were published in Gastroenterology in 2000. 60. Kapp N et al. conducted a systematic review on hormonal contraceptive use among women with liver tumors. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2009. 61. D’halluin V et al. studied the natural history of focal nodular hyperplasia in a retrospective study of 44 cases. Their findings were published in Gastroenterology Clinical Biology in 2001. 62. Aweeka FT et al. investigated the impact of sex and contraceptive therapy on the pharmacokinetics of zidovudine. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2006. 63. Kearney BP et al. found no effect of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate on the pharmacokinetics of hormonal contraceptives. Their findings were published in Pharmacotherapy in 2009. 64. Stuart GS et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of combined oral contraceptives and antiretroviral therapy in Malawian women. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2011. 65. Nanda K et al. found that nevirapine-based antiretroviral therapy does not reduce oral contraceptive effectiveness. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2013. 66. Mildvan D et al. studied the pharmacokinetic interaction between nevirapine and ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone in HIV-infected women. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2002. 67. Landolt NK et al. found that efavirenz, in contrast to nevirapine, is associated with unfavorable progesterone and antiretroviral levels when coadministered with combined oral contraceptives. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2013. 68. Sevinsky H et al. studied the effect of efavirenz on the pharmacokinetics of an oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate in healthy HIV-negative women. Their findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2011.
